t: Deep sleep comes early in the night, and dreams come near morning.
Sleeping late on Sunday cannot fully repair a tired week.
Lena writes tomorrow's jobs on paper before she goes to bed.
People who work at night need to protect their sleep carefully.
Early in the night, each cycle contains a lot of deep sleep and very little dreaming.
Toward morning, the dream stages grow longer, which is why you often wake from a dream.
One myth says that everybody needs exactly eight hours.
Another says that you can fix a week of poor sleep with one long lie-in, but research suggests this only helps a little.
Lying awake, many people go over their worries and tomorrow's tasks.
Writing a short list earlier in the evening can help the mind to put it all down at bedtime.
Shift work and long flights upset the body clock, because they ask you to sleep when it expects daylight.
Dark curtains, planned sleep times and well-timed light can all help you to adjust.
The cycles are not identical, for the early ones are rich in deep sleep and the later ones contain more and longer periods of dreaming.
This is why cutting a night short by two hours takes a disproportionate bite out of the dream stages, which are concentrated near morning.
It is also why people so often wake from a dream just as the alarm rings.
There are several popular myths about sleep, such as the idea that everyone needs exactly eight hours or that older people need hardly any.
Another holds that a long lie-in at the weekend can wipe out the debt from a short week, although research suggests that it repairs only part of the damage.
A steadier pattern is almost always better than a cycle of shortage followed by a binge.
At night the mind loves to rehearse tomorrow's tasks and last week's mistakes, and the darkness makes every item seem heavier.
Lena began to write a short list of tomorrow's jobs and any lingering worries in the early evening, and then close the notebook with a firm click.
The notebook, she told herself, was now holding the problems, and she could safely leave them there until morning.
Night shifts and long flights across time zones ask the body to sleep when its internal clock insists that it should be awake, and the result is the familiar fog of exhaustion.
Blackout curtains, protected sleep times, short strategic naps and carefully timed bright light can all help the clock to adjust.
Even so, long-term shift work is hard on the body, and workers should look after their health with regular check-ups.
Being happy with what you already have is a calm way to live.
Under our anger there is often fear, hurt or being very tired.
Worry makes the same fear go round and round in your head.
Grief is heavy, and it needs time and kind company.
Contentment does not mean giving up your dreams, and it does not mean pretending that everything is perfect.
It means seeing clearly how much good is already here, and enjoying it.
Anger is very often a mask that hides another feeling underneath it.
Behind it you may find hurt feelings, fear or tiredness, and caring for these can calm the anger.
Lena often lay awake at night worrying about things that might go wrong.
Many of the things we fear never happen, and others turn out to be milder than we feared.
When someone we love dies, grief can be heavy and long.
It needs time, kind company and patience, and if it feels too heavy, please speak to a doctor or a counsellor.
Contentment is often misunderstood as laziness or weak ambition, but it is neither of these things.
It is the ability to see clearly how much goodness is already present in your life, and to enjoy it fully while you work towards something more.
A contented person can still plan and strive, yet the peace they feel does not depend on the result.
Anger often wears a mask, and behind it we may find hurt feelings, a hidden fear or simple exhaustion.
When we ask ourselves what is really troubling us, the heat of the anger often fades, because the true cause is finally being looked after.
This kind of honest questioning takes courage, but it saves a great deal of unnecessary conflict.
Lena often lay awake worrying about disasters that had not yet happened and might never do so.
It is a common experience that many of the things we dread never take place, and that others turn out to be milder than we feared.
Worry may feel like sensible preparation for the future, but all too often it is merely suffering in advance of any real trouble.
When we lose someone we love, grief can be heavy, and it follows no timetable.
It needs time, honest tears and the company of kind people, and no spiritual practice should be used to hurry it.
If the sadness feels too heavy to carry, or lasts for a long time, it is wise to seek help from a doctor or counsellor.
Scrooge heard a loud noise, and Marley's ghost came in.
The ghost showed Scrooge the busy streets on Christmas morning.
Poor people sold the dead man's things in a dirty shop.
Scrooge met the kind gentleman and promised him a lot of money.
Scrooge sat by the small fire with a bowl of thin soup.
Suddenly bells began to ring, chains rattled below, and the ghost of Marley walked right through the closed door.
They walked invisibly through the snowy streets, where the shops were full and the people were cheerful.
The Spirit sprinkled drops from his torch over the food as people carried their dinners to the baker's ovens.
In a dark back street, a charwoman, a laundress and an undertaker's man sold a dead man's things to Joe.
They laughed as they took the money, and none of them seemed to care that he had died.
In the street Scrooge met one of the gentlemen who had asked him for money the day before.
He whispered a very large sum in the man's ear, and the gentleman could hardly breathe with surprise.
Scrooge locked himself in, put on his dressing-gown and sat down before his weak fire with a bowl of gruel, but all at once a bell on the wall began to ring, and every bell in the house followed it.
Then came a clanking noise from far below, as if someone were dragging a heavy chain over the cellar floor, and the sound drew steadily nearer.
Without a pause, the ghost of Marley passed through the heavy door and stood in the room, and Scrooge turned cold.

In a moment they were standing in the city, where the snow lay on the roofs and the sooty chimneys and the street was full of cheerful people hurrying along with greetings and brightly coloured parcels.

Grocers' shops were piled with oranges, onions, chestnuts and figs, and the poor carried their dinners to the baker's ovens, while the Spirit sprinkled incense from his torch over the dishes as they passed.
Scrooge, who had always seen Christmas as a waste of time, could not help noticing how bright and joyful it looked to everyone else.
Next the phantom led him to a dark, miserable quarter of the city, where a squalid old shop sold rags and rusted iron, and three people laid out their bundles before the grey-haired owner, Joe.
They had taken the blankets from the dead man's bed, the curtains from the rings, and even his shirt, and they laughed, bargaining over each coin as if it were a prize of war.
Scrooge stood aghast, shuddering at the greed of those who had stripped a man who was no longer alive to complain, and he began to fear that the story was closer to him than he wished.

In the street he met the portly gentleman who had visited his office the day before, and he greeted him with such an overflowing smile that the man, who remembered only his hard words, could scarcely believe it.
When Scrooge whispered in his ear the sum he wished to give, a very large amount, including a number of back payments, the gentleman gasped as if his breath had been taken away.
Scrooge begged him not to say a word of thanks but to come and see him, and the old man promised that he would, and that with a good heart.

Put only fixed times, like a visit, on your calendar.
She reads her email twice a day, not all day.
Keep your system simple, and do not change it often.
One quiet evening, Amara sets aside an hour and writes down everything that is on her mind.
She does not judge or sort anything at this stage, and she simply keeps on writing.
Your calendar is for things that must happen at a certain time, such as a meeting or a visit to the doctor.
Keep it clean, so that you can trust it.
Amara no longer checks her email all day long.
Twice a day, she goes through it and decides what to do with each message.

One quiet evening, Amara sets aside a full hour, sits at the kitchen table with a pen and a large sheet of paper, and writes down everything that is on her mind.
She does not judge, rank or sort any of it at this stage, because the only aim is to get it all out.
When her hand begins to ache, she notices with some surprise that her shoulders have dropped.
Your calendar is a sacred place, reserved for things that must happen at a particular time, such as a meeting, a train or an appointment with the doctor.
If you fill it with wishful intentions, you will soon learn to ignore it, and then you will miss the very things it was meant to protect.
Keep it clean and honest, and it will faithfully keep you on time every day.
Amara no longer checks her email all day long, as though it were a slot machine that might pay out at any moment.
Twice a day she sits down and goes through it, and for each message she decides at once whether to delete it, answer it, file it or turn it into a step on her list.
Her email is a doorway for tasks, and never again a place where she keeps them.
It is tempting to spend whole evenings testing new apps, new colours and new methods, because tinkering feels like progress.
Keep the system as simple as you possibly can, since a plain tool that you use every day is worth far more than a magnificent one that you do not.
The point is to do the work, and not merely to admire the arrangement of it.
Some men sold pills and told stories to scared people.
In summer, the busy streets of London became quiet.
Poor women worked as nurses and helped the sick.
By winter, the plague was almost gone from London.
Fortune tellers, astrologers and quack doctors do good business, because frightened people will pay for any promise.
Printed bills on every corner offer pills, drinks and charms against the plague.
In the heat of the summer, the streets of London fall strangely silent.
Grass begins to grow where crowds used to walk, and only a few frightened people hurry along.
Many poor women work as nurses, taking care of the sick for small pay.
HF says that some are greedy or careless, but he thinks that many are brave and deserve thanks.
With the arrival of the cold winter weather, the plague almost disappears from London.
A few cases continue into the new year, but the Bills show only small numbers now.

Quack doctors, fortune tellers and astrologers found that fear was an excellent business, and their printed bills appeared on every corner, promising pills, drinks and charms that would keep the plague away.
HF is scornful of them, and he warns that many simple people trusted these cheats instead of taking real care, and so exposed themselves to danger.
The more frightened a person became, he observes, the more eagerly he would believe anything he was told by a confident voice.
As the summer heat grew fiercer, the great city became an eerie, half-empty place, with silent markets, shuttered shops and carts that no longer rumbled over the stones.
HF says that grass began to grow in some of the busiest streets, while the few people who still walked about kept to the middle of the road, as far from the houses as they could.
London, once so noisy that a man could not hear his own thoughts, now seemed to be listening.
Nursing the sick was left chiefly to poor women, who took the dangerous work for small pay and often caught the disease themselves.
HF has heard dark stories of nurses who robbed or neglected their patients, yet he doubts that such wickedness was common, and he insists that the greater part of them did their duty bravely.
Many of these women, he believes, deserve a far warmer memory than the stories of that dreadful year have usually given them.
By the middle of winter the plague had almost vanished, though a handful of cases lingered into the new year and kept the careful people watchful.
The weekly Bills, which had once been read with horror, were now read with something close to joy, and the sound of ordinary life returned slowly to the streets.
London, scarred but alive, turned back to the ordinary labour of living, and it began slowly to count what it had lost.

Look at how you spend your days and your money.
Some people will not understand your purpose, and that is fine.
Samuel still misses Ruth, but he feels a little stronger now.
Purpose rarely begins with a grand and carefully drawn plan.
It more often begins when you look up from your own worries and notice what somebody else needs.
Your calendar tells the truth about what you serve.
Look honestly at last week, and ask which hours helped other people and which hours were simply spent.
Some friends and relatives will not understand your choices, and some may laugh at them.
Listen when criticism is fair, but do not let every opinion steer your life.
Samuel still misses his wife every single day, and he does not think that will ever change.
Yet he finds that his sorrow and his new purpose can sit side by side without cancelling each other.
Purpose rarely begins with a grand plan drawn up carefully at a desk by lamplight.
More often it begins in the moment you look up from your own worries and truly see what someone near you is lacking.
Attention, it turns out, is the doorway through which most meaningful work first enters a life.
Your calendar and your bank statement are quiet but honest witnesses to what you actually serve, whatever you may say aloud.
Look closely at the past week, and ask which hours helped someone else, which fed your own growth and which simply disappeared.
There is no need for shame here, only for clear sight, because you cannot steer a ship you refuse to look at.
Some friends and relatives will not understand your choices, and one or two may even laugh at them over dinner.
Listen carefully when the criticism is fair and kindly meant, but do not allow every passing opinion to seize the wheel of your life.
You are the one who must live with the road you take, so choose it with open eyes.
Samuel still misses Ruth every single day, and he no longer expects that the ache will ever fully disappear.
Yet he is discovering that his sorrow and his new purpose can sit quietly side by side, neither one cancelling the other.
Grief, it seems, is simply love that has nowhere else to go, and in time it can find a task.
Many small reasons together can make a day worth starting.
Sleep at regular times, and leave your phone away from the bed.
Rest is not being lazy, and sometimes being tired feels like sadness.
It is never too late to begin something new.
You do not need one great calling to live well.
A few small reasons, each one nothing special alone, can stack together like bricks and hold up a whole day.
Mornings are much easier after a good night's sleep.
Try to go to bed at about the same time each night, and leave your phone on the other side of the room.
Sometimes you are not short of reasons but simply short of sleep.
If you have been working hard or sleeping badly, rest first, and then ask yourself again whether you have a reason.
People are sometimes told that they are too old to begin something new.
It is true that some things become harder, but at any age you can learn, make friends and enjoy a fresh start.
You do not need one overwhelming calling in order to live well, and waiting for one is a good way to waste a decade.
A handful of small reasons, none of them impressive on its own, can be stacked together like bricks until they hold up an entire day.
A sturdy wall does not require a single enormous stone, and neither does a sturdy life, so begin with whatever bricks you have.
Mornings are far easier to face after a decent night's sleep, and sleep is easier when it follows a regular pattern.
Try to go to bed at roughly the same time each evening, and leave your phone charging on the other side of the room, where it cannot tempt you at midnight or ambush you at dawn.
A rested mind is a far more generous judge of the day ahead, and it is quite a bit more likely to find a reason.
Sometimes you are not short of reasons at all but merely short of sleep, and exhaustion can disguise itself very convincingly as despair.
If you have been working hard or sleeping badly for a long time, rest first, and only then ask yourself again whether you have a reason to get up.
Rest is not the enemy of purpose but its foundation, and nobody builds anything lasting while permanently exhausted.
People are sometimes told, or tell themselves, that they are too old to begin something new, and it is true that a few things do become harder with age.
Nevertheless, at almost any age it remains possible to learn, to make new friends and to enjoy the thrill of a fresh start, as every adult education class demonstrates.
The question is rarely whether you can begin, but whether you will allow yourself to, and that decision belongs entirely to you.
Many new doctors still make a promise to help their patients.
Edward Jenner found a safer way to protect people from smallpox.
Sick sailors got better when they ate oranges and lemons.
Some doctors and nurses care for people who cannot be cured.
The Hippocratic Oath is an old promise, and new doctors in many countries still make a version of it.
It asks them to help their patients, to keep their secrets and to protect them from harm.
In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner heard that milkmaids who had caught cowpox seemed safe from smallpox.
He tried the idea on a young boy and it worked, and the word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow.
In 1747 the Scottish naval doctor James Lind gave twelve sick sailors different remedies in six pairs.
The two who ate oranges and lemons got better fastest, but the cause, a lack of vitamin C, was not understood until much later.
Medicine cannot always cure, but it can always care, and Cicely Saunders opened St Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967 to show how.
Her work spread worldwide as palliative care, which aims to ease pain and give comfort and dignity.
The Hippocratic Oath, a short pledge from the ancient Greek world, has been rewritten many times, yet new doctors in many countries still swear a modern version at graduation.
Its central promises are to act for the benefit of the sick, to avoid harming them and to keep their private affairs confidential, and these are the foundations of medical ethics today.
Scholars are not sure who wrote the oldest text, but its influence on the idea of a doctor's duty has been enormous.

In 1796 the English country doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught the mild disease cowpox seemed to escape smallpox, and he tested his idea by giving a boy a little cowpox material and later exposing him to smallpox.
The boy stayed healthy, and although by modern standards the experiment would never be allowed, it launched the age of vaccination, a word taken from the Latin vacca, meaning cow.
Within a few years the method had spread across Europe and beyond, and it was far safer than the older practice of inoculating with smallpox itself.

Scurvy had killed countless sailors on long voyages until, in 1747, the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind divided twelve sick men into six pairs and gave each pair a different remedy, one of which was oranges and lemons.

The two sailors who ate the fruit recovered quickly, which is an early example of a fair comparison, yet it took nearly two centuries before scientists identified vitamin C and explained why the body needs it.
The lesson of scurvy is that a disease can come from a lack of something as well as from a germ.

Medicine cannot always cure, but it can always care, and that conviction led Cicely Saunders, who had trained as a nurse, a social worker and a doctor, to open St Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967.
She taught that pain should be treated seriously and regularly, and that dying people need comfort, company and dignity as much as any other patient needs treatment.
Her ideas spread around the world as palliative care, which today is offered not only at the end of life but alongside treatment for serious illnesses.

They told him that Lucy must marry either Drebber or Stangerson, and that he had thirty days to decide.
The next day Hope found Stangerson at his hotel and offered him the same choice of pills.
Stangerson refused and rushed at him, so Hope stabbed him.
As the weeks passed Watson studied his companion with growing curiosity, for Holmes kept strange hours, played melancholy tunes on his violin and received a bewildering variety of visitors.
His knowledge was extraordinary in some fields, such as chemistry and the history of crime, yet he knew nothing of literature or philosophy and did not even care that the earth goes round the sun.
What, Watson wondered, could such a man possibly do for a living, and why did so many people come to ask his advice?
Late that night a bent old woman shuffled into the room and declared, in a cracked voice, that the ring belonged to her unlucky daughter.
Holmes handed it over without a word and slipped out to follow her, but when at last he caught up with her cab, he found it empty, and he returned in a thoroughly bad mood.
He had been outwitted by a performer cleverer than any he had met in months.
While Hope was away, two stern men, the elders of the community, came to Ferrier's house with a message that would not be refused.
They told him that Lucy must marry either Drebber or Stangerson, both sons of important elders, and that he had exactly thirty days to decide.
Ferrier, who knew very well that disobedience carried a heavy price in that valley, felt his heart sink within him.
The next day Hope found Stangerson at his hotel and offered him the same deadly choice that Drebber had faced, but Stangerson refused and flew at him with his bare hands.
In the struggle that followed Hope drew a knife and stabbed him, and the second man lay dead before the noise had woken the other guests.
Again he wrote the word upon the wall, and then he walked calmly away into the night.
Light is the fastest thing in the world, and nothing is faster.
Jupiter is the biggest planet, and it has a giant storm.
Around a young star, dust joins together to make planets.
In billions of years, Andromeda and our galaxy will merge.
Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second, which is enough to circle Earth seven times in one second.
As far as we know, nothing can go faster.
Jupiter is the biggest planet, so big that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside.
It has no solid ground, only gas, and a great storm that has been seen for at least 150 years.
Around a young star, a spinning disc of dust and gas remains.
Dust sticks together, grows into rocks, and in time becomes planets.
Andromeda is slowly moving towards the Milky Way, and the two galaxies are falling together.
In about four or five billion years, they will probably join into one.
Noor taught Kit the most important number of the tour, the speed of light, which is about 300,000 kilometres every second.
At that speed a beam could race around Earth seven times before you had finished a single blink.
As far as anyone has ever been able to show, nothing in the universe can overtake it.
Jupiter is the giant of the Solar System, large enough to hold more than 1,300 Earths, and it is made almost entirely of gas, with no ground to land on.
Across its stripes of cloud sits the Great Red Spot, a storm wider than our planet.
Astronomers have watched it for at least 150 years, and it is still turning today.
Around every new star there is a spinning disc of leftover gas and dust, and in it, tiny grains stick together and slowly grow into rocks.
Over millions of years, the rocks collide and merge until the largest of them become planets.
Our own Solar System was formed in just this way about four and a half billion years ago.
Andromeda is slowly falling towards the Milky Way, and astronomers think the two galaxies will merge in about four or five billion years.
Stars are so far apart that very few of them will actually collide when the great clouds of stars pass through each other.
The meeting will be less a crash than a slow, glittering dance that lasts for millions of years.
Joints like your knee let your bones bend and move.
Nerve cells send small messages to each other all the time.
Food goes down a tube from your mouth to your stomach.
Sleep gives your body and brain time to rest.
A joint is a place where two bones meet.
The ends of the bones are covered with smooth cartilage and a slippery fluid, so that they glide easily.
A neuron sends a message as a tiny electrical signal along its long fibre.
At the end, a chemical crosses the small gap, called a synapse, and passes the message on to the next cell.
When you swallow, a small flap closes over your windpipe so that food goes down the right way.
Waves of muscle then squeeze it along the oesophagus to your stomach, usually in less than ten seconds.
Everyone needs sleep, and during the night the brain moves through several different stages.
Scientists are still working out exactly why we need sleep, but it clearly helps memory, mood and health.
Wherever two bones meet, there is a joint, and the knee, the hip and the shoulder are among the most remarkable.
The bone ends are capped with cartilage, a smooth, springy material, and the whole joint is bathed in a slippery fluid, so that the surfaces glide past each other with very little friction.
Strong bands called ligaments hold the bones together, allowing movement in some directions while preventing it in others.
A neuron receives signals through its branching fibres and, if they add up to enough, fires a brief electrical pulse along its length.
At the far end, the pulse causes the release of chemical messengers that cross a minute gap, the synapse, and either encourage or discourage the next cell to fire.
Learning, scientists believe, is largely a matter of strengthening some of these connections and weakening others.
Swallowing is a surprisingly complex act in which the tongue pushes food to the back of the mouth, a small flap closes the windpipe and the oesophagus takes over.
Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, then squeeze the food down towards the stomach, and they work so well that you could swallow while standing on your head.
The whole journey from the mouth to the stomach usually takes less than ten seconds in all.
Sleep is not a switching off of the brain but a different kind of activity, in which it passes through repeating cycles of light sleep, deep sleep and dreaming sleep roughly every ninety minutes.
Scientists are still discovering exactly why we need it, although experiments show that it helps to consolidate memories, supports the immune system and keeps mood and attention in order.
Most adults function best on seven to nine hours a night, though the amount varies from person to person.

At midnight Lena and Theo ate toast in the kitchen.
Aunt Dot asked if they were a couple, and both said no.
They ran back, and Lena walked down the aisle with Theo.
On Sunday Ines said the broken parts were the best.
At midnight Lena cannot sleep and goes down to the kitchen, where Theo is making toast.
They argue about whether a wedding needs a list or luck, and then agree to work together for the couple.
Guests arrive all afternoon, and Lena hands out room keys.
Aunt Dot, who is Theo's aunt, asks if the two of them are a couple, and they both say no far too quickly.
Mrs Pruitt has held the ceremony for ten minutes.
Lena and Theo hurry in, sandy and breathless, and walk down the aisle together with the ring box in Theo's pocket.
At Sunday breakfast Ines sits next to Lena and teases her about Theo.
She says that the best parts of her wedding were the parts that went wrong.
At midnight Lena crept down to the kitchen and found Theo buttering toast at the steel counter, as though he had every right to be there.
They argued in whispers about whether a wedding needed a list or a little luck, each convinced the other was wrong, until he pushed a slice across the table.
For Ines and Sam's sake, they agreed, they would work together, and for the first time that evening their smiles were real.
All through the afternoon the guests arrived in noisy waves, and Lena gave out room keys, name tags and directions to the sea.
Theo's Aunt Dot, a round and cheerful woman who missed nothing, narrowed her eyes at the pair of them and asked whether they were by any chance a couple.
They both answered no at exactly the same moment, a little too loudly, and Aunt Dot smiled to herself and went to find her room.
Mrs Pruitt, stern as a general, had held the ceremony for ten minutes by announcing that the music was still being tuned.
Lena and Theo slipped into place at the head of the aisle, breathless and covered in sand, and walked down between the rows of smiling guests with the ring box safe in his pocket.
Lena had one bare foot and one shoe, and for once she did not care who noticed.
At Sunday breakfast, with the guests sleepy and hoarse from dancing, Ines slid onto the bench beside Lena and teased her gently about the best man.
She said that the best parts of her wedding had been the broken ones, and that if Lena had made it perfect, she would never have laughed so hard or fallen so well.
A list, Ines added with a smile, was a lovely thing, but it had never yet kissed anybody.

For most of history nobody could see a planet around another star, but in 1995 astronomers found the first one circling a star like the Sun.
Planets outside our Solar System are now called exoplanets, and the search for them has become one of the busiest and most exciting fields in astronomy.

They had linked radio telescopes across the world to make a single instrument the size of the Earth, and in 2022 they did the same for the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy.
A thing that cannot be seen had at last been photographed by the glow of its surroundings, which is a remarkable achievement.

Archer stops in the middle of the street, so surprised and moved that he cannot speak.

At home, Newland lived with his mother and his sister Janey, two gentle women who knew every rule of old New York and obeyed it without complaint.
Their world was polite, comfortable and orderly, and what mattered most in it was that certain things should never be said, because to speak of them would make them real.
Newland loved his family and respected its customs, yet he sometimes wondered whether anyone had ever stepped outside the pattern to see what lay beyond.
When Ellen slipped away to Boston, Archer followed her on the next train, and found her sitting alone in the Public Garden beside the still water.
For the first time they spoke openly of what lay between them, and each saw the same longing in the other's eyes.

The house around him, with its fine furniture and soft carpets, seemed suddenly very quiet.

The Inca built a vast network of roads, with stone steps and rope bridges across deep valleys.
Relay runners called chasqui carried messages from one station to the next, day and night.
On the northwest Pacific coast, people lived very well without farming, because the rivers were full of salmon.
They built plank houses and canoes from cedar trees, and they carved tall poles that told family stories.
The newcomers carried diseases such as smallpox and measles, which had never reached the Americas before.
People had built up no protection against them, and the illnesses often spread faster than the Europeans did.
In many regions, farmers planted maize, beans and squash together, a combination that suited the three plants and their growers equally well.

The beans climbed the maize stalks and added nitrogen to the soil, the broad squash leaves shaded the ground and discouraged weeds, and together the three crops gave people a diet that was balanced in energy and protein.
Few agricultural systems anywhere in the world show such elegant cooperation between different species.

The Inca linked their mountainous empire with a network of roads that ran for tens of thousands of kilometres, climbing cliffs by stone stairways and crossing gorges on bridges woven from grass ropes.
Along these roads, relay runners called chasqui passed messages from station to station, so that news could cross a huge distance in a few days.
People travelled on foot, with llamas carrying the goods, because there were no horses or wheeled carts.

Along the rainy northwest coast, from Alaska to Oregon, peoples such as the Haida and the Tlingit built rich societies without farming, because the rivers produced huge runs of salmon that could be smoked and stored for the winter.

Skilled carpenters used red cedar to make plank houses, ocean-going canoes and tall carved poles that recorded family histories, and great feasts called potlatches marked important events and shared wealth.
These prosperous communities had strict ranks and artists of exceptional skill, and their work is admired around the world today.
The Europeans carried diseases such as smallpox, measles and influenza, which had been unknown in the Americas, and a people who had never met them had no immunity and died in terrible numbers.
Epidemics often travelled along trade routes ahead of the newcomers, so that some communities were struck by disease before they had ever seen a European.
In many regions, villages lost so many people that fields went untended and the survivors could not carry on their old ways of life.

Rule by orders and punishments, Confucius warned, produces people who learn only to avoid the penalty, and who feel no shame about the wrong itself.
Lead them instead by example and by courtesy, and they will develop a sense of shame and, of their own accord, set themselves right.
His faith was in the power of character to change a community from the inside, which no threat could ever do from the outside.
Zigong, the eloquent student, once asked what Confucius would say of a person who could bring benefit to all the people and help everyone around him: could he be called humane?
Such a person, the teacher replied, would be far more than humane, a sage, for even the legendary kings Yao and Shun would have found it hard to do so much.
The humane person, he added, simply helps others to stand firm and to succeed, wishing for them what he wishes for himself.
The eleventh book also holds one of the saddest moments in the Analects, the death of Yan Hui, the student whom Confucius loved best.
The old teacher cried out that Heaven had destroyed him, and he wept so bitterly that his followers told him he was grieving too much.
Was that so, he asked, and for whom should he grieve, if not for such a man?
Preparation is the quiet subject of two short sayings in the fifteenth book, and both urge us to look ahead.
A craftsman who wishes to do his work well, Confucius says, must first sharpen his tools, and he gave this advice to a student who had asked how to live a humane life.
He adds a warning to the same effect: anyone who does not think about what lies far ahead will find sorrow waiting close at hand.

Each day he ate about twelve ounces of food and drank about fourteen ounces of wine.
Cornaro returned to his old measure of food and wine.
He soon recovered, and after that he never changed it again.
For Cornaro, the sober life was not only about food.
It meant moderation in everything, in eating, in drinking, in work, in sleep and in feelings.
Cornaro died in the city of Padua in the year 1566.
Accounts say that he died peacefully in his chair, but we do not know his exact age.
Cornaro made himself a strict rule for eating and drinking, and he measured it carefully by weight.
Every day, he says, he took about twelve ounces of solid food and about fourteen ounces of wine, an ounce being a small weight of roughly thirty grams in modern terms.
That is a small amount, and it should be remembered that it was his own choice, not a recommendation for every person.
He went back immediately to his old measure, and in a short time, he says, he was well again.
The experience convinced him that the rule suited his own body, and he never again allowed his friends to talk him out of it.
Whether the extra food was really the cause of his illness, nobody can say for certain.
By the sober life, Cornaro meant something wider than careful eating, for it covered every part of ordinary living, including work, rest, sleep and the passions of the heart.
In each of these, the aim was to avoid both too much and too little, and to keep the body and mind in a steady balance.
This ancient idea of the middle path is found in many traditions, and Cornaro made it practical.
Cornaro died in Padua in 1566, and later accounts say that he passed away peacefully in his chair, without a long illness.
His exact age cannot be known because the year of his birth is uncertain, but he was certainly very old, perhaps close to one hundred.
If so, he lived far longer than most of his neighbours and contemporaries did in that age.

Barnum wrote that money is like fire, a very good servant but a terrible master.
He believed that anyone can learn to earn it, if they follow some simple rules.
Barnum said that an owner should look for the best helpers and then pay them fairly.
Workers who are paid well and treated kindly are likely to stay and to serve the business well.
Barnum, the great showman, said that every business should advertise.
A shop may be excellent, but people will not come if they have never heard of it.
Taken together, Barnum's rules form a kind of path from start to finish.
First you choose the right work, then you work hard and keep order, and last you treat others honestly.
Barnum begins from a plain belief, which is that anyone willing to learn and to work can follow the road to wealth, whatever the starting point.
Money, he wrote, is in some respects like fire, for it is an excellent servant but a terrible master, and he wanted his readers to command it rather than be commanded by it.
His twenty or so rules, taken one at a time, are meant to show how.
Having found good people, Barnum argued, an employer should reward them fairly, for a worker who feels that he is properly paid is likely to give honest and willing service.
A business that is always changing its staff to save a few dollars, he warned, pays the cost in mistakes and lost customers.
It is better to keep a skilled assistant on a generous wage than to hire a stranger on a poor one.
As a showman, Barnum was a master of publicity, and he insisted that every business owner should advertise, since no shop can serve customers who do not know it exists.
The finest goods, honestly priced, will still lie unsold on the shelves if nobody is told about them.
A man who hides his light under a bushel, he implied, has only himself to blame when others pass by.

Read together, Barnum's rules fall into a natural order, beginning with the choice of work and place, moving through the habits of energy, system and prudence, and ending with courtesy, generosity and honesty toward others.
Each rule supports the others, for a person who keeps out of debt can afford to be honest, and a person who is honest earns the trust that brings customers.
They are less a list of tricks than a description of a steady, practical character.

Sun Tzu says that attacking a walled city is a last choice, used only when there is no other way.

The one who arrives later must hurry, and he comes already tired.
In the chapter on terrain, Sun Tzu says that a commander who treats his soldiers like his own children will be followed anywhere.

The fourth factor is the commander himself, who must combine wisdom, trustworthiness, kindness, courage and strictness.
These qualities pull against each other, so the real skill lies in balance: too much kindness makes an army soft, and too much strictness makes it afraid.
A plan is only as good as the person who has to carry it out.
A siege, Sun Tzu warns, is the worst of the options, because it takes months to prepare and a general who loses patience throws his men against the walls in waves.
A large part of his army may be lost, and the city may still be standing at the end of it.
Cities should therefore be attacked only when nothing else will do, and then only with a clear reason.
In the sixth chapter, Sun Tzu points out that whoever occupies the field first and awaits the enemy there will be fresh, while whoever arrives second and rushes into battle will be exhausted.

Loyalty is earned by both care and discipline, and either one without the other will fail.

He would be an apprentice until the age of twenty-one.

He bought three large rolls and walked up Market Street with one under each arm, eating the third.
Benjamin knew that a young businessman must be trusted, so he dressed plainly and avoided fun that wasted time.
He even pushed paper through the streets on a wheelbarrow, so that everyone could see how hard he worked.
Philadelphia's streets were covered in mud, so Benjamin helped to arrange for them to be paved and swept.

James Franklin had come home from England with a printing press and a set of type, and Josiah agreed that his youngest son should learn the trade from him.

A young woman named Deborah Read stood at her father's door and laughed at the sight, and years later she became his wife.

Krishna smiles and tells Arjuna not to grieve so much.
One who acts without clinging is like a leaf the water cannot touch.
Arjuna sees a light as bright as a thousand suns.
Words should be true, kind, and good for the listener.
Krishna answers gently, and he says that this weakness does not suit a man like Arjuna.
The wise, he says, do not grieve for the living or for the dead, for there is something in us that does not die.
Arjuna asks whether it is better to give up action or to do it with the right attitude.
Krishna says that both lead to freedom, and that one who acts without clinging is like a lotus leaf untouched by water.
Arjuna sees the whole universe in Krishna's body, with countless mouths, eyes and arms and a light as bright as a thousand suns.
His hair stands on end, and he bows with folded hands, trembling with wonder.
Krishna also describes the discipline of speech, which he treats as a form of self-training.
Words that cause no pain and that are true, pleasant and helpful belong to this discipline.
Krishna answers with a gentle smile, saying that this weakness of the heart is unworthy of a man such as Arjuna and that he should stand up and put it away.
You grieve for those who need no grief, he says, and yet you speak the language of wisdom, for the wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.
So begins the long teaching of the Gita, which starts, strangely enough, with the question of what a person really is.

In the fifth chapter Arjuna asks whether it is better to renounce action or to practise the Yoga of action, and Krishna replies that both lead to the highest goal, though the Yoga of action is the easier.
The person who offers his actions to the divine and abandons all attachment, he says, is untouched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is untouched by the water on it.
His body, mind and senses work, but he works only for the purification of the self and does not cling to the fruit.
Arjuna beholds the whole universe gathered into one body, with countless mouths, eyes and arms, wearing heavenly garlands and dazzling with a splendour like a thousand suns rising at once in the sky.
His hair stands on end, and he bows his head with folded hands, trembling with wonder, awe and a little fear.
He sees the gods, the sages and all creatures within that form, and he understands that what he took to be a single friend is the ground of everything.
Among the disciplines that Krishna describes in this chapter is the discipline of speech, which he places beside the discipline of the body and the discipline of the mind.
Speech, he says, should not cause distress, and it should be truthful, pleasant and helpful, and it should be accompanied by the regular study of sacred texts.
Calmness, gentleness, silence, self-control and purity of heart are the matching discipline of the mind.

Carnegie later gathered it into a book of essays that carried the same name, and the book spread his ideas still further.
Carnegie went so far as to approve heavy taxes on large inheritances, calling death duties the wisest of all forms of taxation.

By taxing great estates at death, he said, the state marks its condemnation of the selfish millionaire's unworthy life, and gives wealthy people a strong reason to put their money to use while they are alive.
It was a remarkably bold thing for a millionaire to say in public, since many wealthy men of his day were deeply suspicious of any new tax.

If some of them beat the average, others must fall short of it by the same amount, and once the fees are taken, the average professional lags behind.
This is simple arithmetic rather than a matter of opinion, and it explains why beating the market is so hard.
